units.translation: 153. If you should drive it in: if you should thrust it in, lay it upon.
7 ἐνερείσῃς in Hoelzlin : -ργήσῃς ἐπιβάλῃς in P (A) H : -οις in L
166. Up through the aether: instead of 'up through the aether' (accusative), dative instead of accusative. LmP
8 τοῦ ἀν’ in P : omitted in L; πολλὸν ἰόντι added before δοτικὴ in L, which K wishes to be added to the lemma
167. His own: one should have said 'their own' (σφῆς), so that it would be 'of themselves'; but 'his own' (ἑῆς) is 'of himself'. Lm (P)
173. 〈For the need is common:〉 for the need and the words are common. Lm
174-75. But he silently his mind: but he who acts in silence and hides in himself what is advantageous, this man takes away our safety. L
14 the codex at the end adds: παραιρεῖται instead of 'does not wish'; for παρὰ changed the αἱρεῖται. cf. W 53
186. Their own possession: 'their own' (σφέτερον) is not correct; for it is third person plural. And he errs; for it should be singular and not plural: 'to take away his own possession'.
187. Better: 'λωίτερον' itself is comparative of 'λῶον'; but 'λωίτερον' is derived for the sake of the meter.
18 αὐτὸ τὸ in L : ἀπὸ τοῦ in PA

190-91. This man once blameless: with an acute accent on the first syllable; for it is said with reference to Aeetes. And the order is: 'this man once received Phrixus fleeing from his father's sacrifices'.
20 διὰ in W : ἀπὸ : ἐπὶ in Schaefer
21 τοῦ Αἰήτου in F : τόν Αἰήτην in P : τόν Πελίαν in L
199. On the bank of the plain: of the place lying above the river, where it is possible to leap and jump from the ship. LGm (P)
24 199. Etymologicum Genuinum (B) χέρσονδ’ ἐξαποβάντες: a local adverb, instead of 'to the land', as 'to Ilium' (Ἰλιόνδε)
25 θορεῖν καὶ πηδῆσαι in L : θεωρεῖν καὶ πηδᾶν in G : θροεῖν καὶ πηδᾶν in P

200a. Circe's, that indeed: some say Circe is the sister of Aeetes, others the daughter. Dionysius (32 F 1a J.) records that from Helios were born Perseus and Aeetes. Perseus ruled over the Tauri and having consorted with a certain nymph, Hecate, had a daughter, who, spending her time in the deserts on each occasion, became most experienced in both poisons and things able to heal; whom Aeetes sent for and married, and had from her Circe.
